mil5.1.7:0.4: 7. Question on the Disappearance of the True Teaching
mil5.1.7:1.1: “Venerable Nāgasena, this too was spoken by the Blessed One:
mil5.1.7:1.2: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:1.3: And again, at the time of his final Nibbāna, when the wanderer Subhadda asked a question, the Blessed One said:
mil5.1.7:1.4: ‘If these monks, Subhadda, were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of arahants.’ This statement is without remainder, without exception, and without qualification.
mil5.1.7:1.5: If, Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata said,
mil5.1.7:1.6: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years,’ then the statement ‘the world would not be empty of arahants’ is false.
mil5.1.7:1.8: ‘the world would not be empty of arahants,’ then the statement ‘the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years’ is also false.
mil5.1.7:1.9: This is a two-horned dilemma. It is more tangled than the tangled, stronger than the strong, more knotted than the knotted. It has now come to you. Show here the power and range of your wisdom, like a sea-monster that has gone into the middle of the ocean.”
mil5.1.7:2.1: “This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, your majesty: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:2.2: And at the time of his final Nibbāna, he said to the wanderer Subhadda:
mil5.1.7:2.3: ‘If these monks, Subhadda, were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of arahants.’
mil5.1.7:2.4: But those words of the Blessed One, your majesty, differ in meaning and differ in phrasing. The one is a limit placed on the Dispensation; the other is an exposition of practice. The two are far removed from each other.
